cards.front: In the extracellular matrix, collagen acts as a structural rope while {{c1::fibronectin}} acts as a glue that binds collagen with one part and cells with another.
cards.quote: Collagen is its rope; fibronectin is one of its glues, sticking to collagen with one part and to cells with another.
cards.section: The idea: a receptor for something solid

cards.front: The minimal three-amino-acid handle on fibronectin recognised by integrins is {{c1::RGD}} (Arg-Gly-Asp).
cards.back: Derived from the four-residue Arg-Gly-Asp-Ser cell-binding sequence.
cards.quote: The first three—RGD in one-letter code—are the handle.
cards.section: The idea: a receptor for something solid

cards.front: What is the basic architecture of an integrin receptor?
cards.back: A heterodimer of single-pass α and β chains with an extracellular matrix-binding head, short cytoplasmic tails (a few dozen amino acids in nearly every case), and no intrinsic kinase or channel.
cards.why: Linker proteins connect the short cytoplasmic tails to actin filaments, while recruited cytoplasmic kinases provide signalling activity.
cards.quote: An integrin is a heterodimer of two different chains, α and β, each crossing the membrane once.
cards.section: The idea: a receptor for something solid

cards.front: Short synthetic Arg-Gly-Asp-Ser fragments substitute for fibronectin's cell-binding region, and adding soluble RGD peptide to a fibronectin-coated dish reduces the fraction of attached cells. What does this demonstrate?
cards.back: Cells grip fibronectin through a short specific sequence (RGD), and free peptide competitively fills the integrin binding site so fewer receptors can hold the matrix.
cards.quote: Add enough free RGD peptide to a dish and fewer cells hold on to fibronectin, because the peptide fills the site the matrix would have filled.
cards.section: The idea: a receptor for something solid

cards.front: High concentrations of soluble RGD peptide are added to fibroblasts plated on fibronectin and separately to cells plated on collagen bound by non-RGD integrins. What happens to attachment in each dish, and why?
cards.back: Attachment drops sharply on fibronectin but remains largely intact on collagen. Free RGD competes directly for the binding cleft of RGD-recognising integrins, whereas integrins gripping collagen at non-RGD sites do not use that handle.
cards.quote: Integrins gripping collagen through non-RGD sites do not use that handle, so free RGD leaves their attachment largely intact.
cards.section: The idea: a receptor for something solid

cards.front: Unlike canonical integrins that connect to actin filaments, the integrin {{c1::α6β4}} links to keratin filaments instead.
cards.quote: one integrin, α6β4, links to keratin filaments instead
cards.section: The idea: a receptor for something solid

cards.front: Why do cells regulate integrin binding from inside the cell instead of waiting for ligand arrival, as hormone receptors do?
cards.back: Many integrins are bathed in extracellular ligand continuously, so preventing unwanted adhesion requires keeping the receptor itself in a low-affinity state until an internal signal activates it.
cards.quote: A hormone receptor waits for its ligand; an integrin is often bathed in ligand continuously, so the cell controls the receptor instead.
cards.section: A grip that is switched on from inside

cards.front: How does talin switch a resting platelet or leukocyte integrin from weak grip to tight grip during inside-out signalling?
cards.back: Talin binds the β tail and pries the packed α and β tails and transmembrane segments apart, straightening the bent outer legs and opening the head into a tight grip.
cards.why: In the resting state, tight α–β tail and transmembrane packing keeps the outer legs folded at a knee with the closed head tipped toward the membrane.
cards.quote: talin binds the β tail and pries the α and β tails and membrane segments apart
cards.section: A grip that is switched on from inside

cards.front: In addition to talin, a second β-tail-binding protein called {{c1::kindlin}} is required for inside-out integrin activation.
cards.quote: A second β-tail-binding protein, kindlin, is needed as well.
cards.section: A grip that is switched on from inside

cards.front: A mutation disrupts packing between the α and β transmembrane segments of a platelet integrin so the tails separate without talin. What happens to the outer head and to circulating platelets, and why?
cards.back: The outer head shifts toward its extended, high-affinity state, causing platelets to bind circulating fibrinogen without a wound and initiate inappropriate clumping. Separating the transmembrane segments mimics inside-out activation.
cards.quote: Uncoupling the tails should shift the integrin toward its extended, high-affinity state without any inside signal.
cards.section: A grip that is switched on from inside

cards.front: Once wound signals activate integrins on platelets at a cut vessel, how does fibrinogen assemble a platelet plug?
cards.back: Platelet integrins switch on within seconds and grip two-ended fibrinogen molecules, which bridge neighbouring platelets together into a plug.
cards.why: While blood flows normally, those platelet integrins stay switched off despite continuous exposure to circulating fibrinogen.
cards.quote: At a cut vessel, wound signals switch αIIbβ3 on within seconds, and two-ended fibrinogen bridges platelets into a plug.
cards.section: A grip that is switched on from inside

cards.front: At a focal adhesion, {{c1::paxillin}} serves as an enzyme-free scaffold crowded with docking sites.
cards.quote: paxillin is an enzyme-free scaffold crowded with docking sites; and focal adhesion kinase (FAK) is a tyrosine kinase recruited from the cytoplasm
cards.section: The focal adhesion: a signalling machine that can feel a pull

cards.front: How does an integrin initiate intracellular tyrosine phosphorylation despite lacking an intrinsic kinase domain?
cards.back: Clustered integrins assemble a focal adhesion that borrows a cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase (FAK), which opens, autophosphorylates, and recruits a second kinase (Src) to phosphorylate nearby adhesion proteins.
cards.why: This borrowing strategy parallels cytokine receptors that lack kinase domains and recruit cytoplasmic JAKs.
cards.quote: With no enzyme of its own, an integrin borrows one, much as cytokine receptors borrow JAKs in the JAK and STAT lesson.
cards.section: The focal adhesion: a signalling machine that can feel a pull

cards.front: How are FAK and Src sequentially activated once integrins cluster at a focal adhesion?
cards.back: FAK unfolds from its closed FERM-against-kinase state and autophosphorylates Tyr397; phosphorylated Tyr397 docks the SH2 domain of Src, which phosphorylates FAK further so both kinases phosphorylate neighbouring scaffolds.
cards.why: The added phosphotyrosines create new docking sites on proteins such as paxillin and recruit adaptors such as Grb2 on FAK.
cards.quote: Resting FAK is folded shut, with its FERM domain lying against its kinase domain. At a cluster of integrins it opens and phosphorylates itself on Tyr397
cards.section: The focal adhesion: a signalling machine that can feel a pull

cards.front: Cells express a mutant focal adhesion kinase (FAK) in which its autophosphorylation site (Tyr397) is replaced by phenylalanine, yet they still adhere to fibronectin. Which signalling step fails first, and why?
cards.back: Docking of Src onto FAK fails first. Phenylalanine cannot be phosphorylated, so FAK cannot create the phosphotyrosine site required to bind the SH2 domain of Src.
cards.why: Matrix attachment persists because extracellular binding by the integrin head does not depend on FAK phosphorylation.
cards.quote: Phosphorylated Tyr397 docks the SH2 domain of Src; docked Src phosphorylates FAK further, and the pair phosphorylates neighbours such as paxillin to add more docking sites.
cards.section: The focal adhesion: a signalling machine that can feel a pull

cards.front: Cells kept in suspension are incubated with soluble RGD peptide rather than immobilized fibronectin, so integrins bind ligand one-to-one without clustering. What happens to FAK–Src signalling, and why?
cards.back: Strong FAK–Src signalling does not occur. Monovalent binding in solution fails to cluster integrin tails laterally, so FAK is not gathered to unfold, autophosphorylate Tyr397, and recruit Src.
cards.quote: One-to-one binding in solution does not cluster integrin tails, so FAK is not gathered to open, phosphorylate Tyr397 and recruit Src.
cards.section: The focal adhesion: a signalling machine that can feel a pull

cards.front: Why does the mechanical layout of a focal adhesion enable a cell to distinguish a stiff surface from a soft one?
cards.back: Matrix, integrin, talin, and myosin-pulled actin sit in series, so a stiff surface resists myosin pull and builds tension across talin, whereas a soft surface yields.
cards.quote: Because its parts sit in series—matrix ↔ integrin ↔ talin ↔ actin pulled by myosin—the adhesion also measures force.
cards.section: The focal adhesion: a signalling machine that can feel a pull

cards.front: When fibronectin-coated beads on fibroblasts were held against cellular pulling with an optical trap, stronger trap resistance caused cells to tie those integrins more firmly to actin. What did this show?
cards.back: Integrin–actin linkages actively reinforce in response to mechanical resistance rather than acting as static tethers.
cards.quote: held fibronectin-coated beads on fibroblasts with an optical trap (laser tweezers): the harder the trap resisted, the more firmly the cell tied those integrins to actin.
cards.section: The focal adhesion: a signalling machine that can feel a pull

cards.front: A purified talin rod tethered between glass and a magnetic bead binds at most one fluorescent vinculin head when unpulled, but binds up to three at about 12 pN, with no phosphate added and no GTP exchanged. What does this show?
cards.back: Mechanical force alone unfolds talin helix bundles to expose buried vinculin-binding sites, converting physical tension directly into protein binding without phosphorylation or GTP exchange.
cards.why: In living cells, full-length vinculin recruited to stretched talin also grips actin filaments, reinforcing pulled adhesions.
cards.quote: No phosphate was added and no GTP was exchanged: force alone exposed buried sites.
cards.section: The focal adhesion: a signalling machine that can feel a pull

cards.front: Fibroblasts are plated on a soft fibronectin gel, on stiff fibronectin-coated glass, or on stiff glass with a myosin II blocker. How do talin stretching and vinculin recruitment compare, and why?
cards.back: Talin stretches and recruits vinculin strongly only on stiff glass without the blocker; both the soft gel and myosin II inhibition leave talin slack and prevent reinforcement. Tension requires both internal myosin pull and external resistance.
cards.quote: Blocking myosin II removes internal pull even on stiff glass, leaving talin slack so adhesions fail to reinforce.
cards.section: The focal adhesion: a signalling machine that can feel a pull

cards.front: A cell completely lacking talin is placed on stiff fibronectin-coated glass. Combining the inside-out switch and focal-adhesion rules, predict what happens to integrin affinity, FAK–Src signalling, and force-dependent vinculin recruitment.
cards.back: All three are impaired: without talin to separate α and β tails, integrins stay low-affinity; reduced binding and clustering blunts FAK–Src activation; and without talin bridging β tails to actin, tension cannot expose vinculin sites. This rests on talin's dual role as inside-out activator and series force transducer.
cards.quote: talin joins the β tail to actin; vinculin binds both talin and actin to reinforce the join
cards.section: The focal adhesion: a signalling machine that can feel a pull

cards.front: Like Ras, small GTPases of the Rho family cycle between active GTP-bound and inactive GDP-bound states regulated by {{c1::GEFs and GAPs}}.
cards.quote: small GTPases of the Rho family that cycle between GTP-bound ("on") and GDP-bound ("off") states via GEFs and GAPs, like Ras.
cards.section: Three switches for the actin skeleton

cards.front: Among the three canonical Rho-family switches, {{c1::Rho}} drives assembly of contractile actin–myosin II stress fibres ending in focal adhesions.
cards.quote: Stress fibres: contractile actin–myosin II cables ending in focal adhesions
cards.section: Three switches for the actin skeleton

cards.front: Among the three canonical Rho-family switches, {{c1::Rac}} builds sheet-like lamellipodia pushed forward by a branching actin mesh.
cards.quote: Lamellipodia: broad sheets pushed by a branching actin mesh
cards.section: Three switches for the actin skeleton

cards.front: Among the three canonical Rho-family switches, {{c1::Cdc42}} is classically linked to thin finger-like filopodia containing parallel actin cores.
cards.quote: Filopodia: thin fingers with parallel actin cores
cards.section: Three switches for the actin skeleton

cards.front: Which key effector connects active Rho to stress-fibre contraction, and how else is Rho coupled?
cards.back: Rho activates Rho kinase (ROCK), which raises myosin II activity; Rho can also engage formins for unbranched filaments and be activated upstream by G12/13-coupled GPCRs.
cards.quote: Rho kinase (ROCK) raises myosin II activity (formins also build unbranched filaments)
cards.section: Three switches for the actin skeleton

cards.front: Through which effectors does active Rac build the branching actin mesh of a lamellipodium?
cards.back: Rac-GTP activates the WAVE complex, which turns on Arp2/3 so each new actin filament nucleates as a branch off an existing filament.
cards.quote: WAVE complex turns on Arp2/3, starting each new filament as a branch
cards.section: Three switches for the actin skeleton

cards.front: Which effector does Cdc42-GTP activate, and what nuance explains how filopodia acquire parallel actin cores?
cards.back: Cdc42-GTP opens folded WASP or N-WASP to activate Arp2/3 (which nucleates branched actin), whereas elongating parallel filopodial cores relies mainly on formins and Ena/VASP proteins.
cards.why: In living cells, some filopodia can even form without Cdc42 or N-WASP.
cards.quote: Notice the Cdc42 nuance: Arp2/3 nucleates branched actin, whereas filopodia have parallel cores.
cards.section: Three switches for the actin skeleton

cards.front: In serum-starved fibroblasts that initially lack stress fibres, microinjecting active Rho produces thick actin cables and focal adhesions, active Rac causes edge ruffling, and active Cdc42 produces thin spikes. What does this show?
cards.back: Each active Rho-family GTPase is sufficient on its own to drive a distinct actin cytoskeletal structure in these fibroblasts.
cards.quote: active Rho filled them with thick actin cables and focal adhesions, and active Rac made their edges ruffle.
cards.section: Three switches for the actin skeleton

cards.front: Active Rac-GTP is present at a fibroblast's leading edge, but a genetic deletion eliminates Arp2/3. What happens to lamellipodium assembly, and why?
cards.back: A branching lamellipodium cannot form. Even when Rac-GTP activates the WAVE complex, downstream Arp2/3 is required to nucleate each new actin filament as a branch.
cards.quote: Without Arp2/3, Rac-GTP and WAVE cannot nucleate the branching mesh of a lamellipodium.
cards.section: Three switches for the actin skeleton

cards.front: A fibroblast expresses Rho locked in its GTP-bound state while a drug directly inhibits myosin II. What happens to stress-fibre contraction, and why?
cards.back: Stress-fibre contraction is prevented. Myosin II is the contractile motor acting downstream of Rho and ROCK, so blocking myosin II directly overrides continuous upstream Rho-GTP activity.
cards.quote: Likewise, active Rho cannot drive contraction if myosin II itself is blocked downstream of ROCK.
cards.section: Three switches for the actin skeleton

cards.front: A researcher hypothesises that a Rho-family GTPase mediates stress-fibre formation after an extracellular lipid signal in serum-starved fibroblasts. Using the small-GTPase switch rules, design a two-part perturbation experiment to test whether the GTPase is both necessary and sufficient.
cards.back: To test necessity, inactivate the GTPase before adding the lipid signal; stress fibres should fail to form. To test sufficiency, introduce the GTPase locked in its GTP-bound state without the lipid; stress fibres should form. This rests on the rule that Rho-family GTPases switch on when GTP-bound and off when inactivated.
cards.quote: In 1992 Anne Ridley and Alan Hall injected purified proteins into serum-starved fibroblasts, which have few stress fibres
cards.section: Three switches for the actin skeleton

cards.front: What four coordinated phases advance a fibroblast across a fibronectin-coated surface?
cards.back: Push out a lamellipodium (Rac), grip the matrix with new front adhesions, pull the cell body forward via actomyosin contraction (Rho/ROCK/myosin II), and let go by disassembling rear adhesions.
cards.why: Live-cell sensors refine the simple Rac-front/Rho-back view by detecting Rho activity at the leading edge too.
cards.quote: refining the "Rac in front, Rho behind" first model with live-cell sensors that also detect Rho at the leading edge.
cards.section: How a cell crawls, and what happens when it cannot

cards.front: A migrating fibroblast carries a FAK Tyr397-to-phenylalanine mutation that prevents Src docking while allowing initial matrix attachment. Combining the focal-adhesion and Rac pathways, predict the effect on leading-edge lamellipodium feedback, and why.
cards.back: Positive feedback driving leading-edge Rac protrusion weakens. By the rules that FAK–Src phosphorylates adhesion proteins and that phosphorylated adhesion proteins recruit Rac GEFs, losing Src docking on FAK curtails local Rac activation at new front adhesions.
cards.quote: grip (new front adhesions feeding back through FAK/Src to Rac GEFs)
cards.section: How a cell crawls, and what happens when it cannot

cards.front: A fibroblast plated on stiff fibronectin-coated glass is treated with a drug that inhibits Rho kinase (ROCK). Combining the Rho effector pathway with focal-adhesion mechanosensing, predict what happens to talin tension and vinculin recruitment, and why.
cards.back: Talin remains slack and adhesions fail to recruit vinculin for reinforcement. By the rules that ROCK elevates myosin II activity and that stiff substrates stretch talin only against internal myosin pull, blocking ROCK eliminates the pull needed to uncover vinculin sites.
cards.quote: Both halves of the lesson's rule now meet: inside-out integrin grip and force-sensing adhesions work with Rho, Rac and Cdc42 to drive crawling.
cards.section: How a cell crawls, and what happens when it cannot

cards.front: Suppose a mutation locks a fibroblast's integrins permanently in their high-affinity state so rear adhesions cannot disassemble, while Rac protrusion and Rho contraction remain normal. Predict what happens to net crawling, and explain.
cards.back: Net forward crawling stalls. By the crawling-cycle rule that cells must push, grip, pull, and let go, rear adhesions that cannot dissolve keep the tail anchored despite leading-edge protrusion and actomyosin pulling.
cards.quote: pull (Rho, ROCK and myosin II hauling the body forward) and let go (rear adhesions dissolving so the tail draws in)
cards.section: How a cell crawls, and what happens when it cannot

cards.front: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type I (LAD-I) stems from a mutation in the {{c1::β2}} (ITGB2) subunit shared by white-cell integrins, preventing leukocytes from stopping on vessel walls.
cards.back: Causes severe bacterial infections from infancy and can be cured by bone marrow transplant.
cards.quote: A mutation in β2 (ITGB2), shared by white-cell β2 integrins, keeps white cells from stopping on vessel walls, causing severe bacterial infections from infancy.
cards.section: How a cell crawls, and what happens when it cannot

cards.front: People with {{c1::Glanzmann thrombasthenia}} lack functional platelet αIIbβ3 integrins, so platelets cannot be bridged by fibrinogen and patients bleed easily.
cards.quote: Glanzmann thrombasthenia: People lacking working platelet αIIbβ3 cannot bridge platelets with fibrinogen and bleed easily.
cards.section: How a cell crawls, and what happens when it cannot

cards.front: A patient undergoing a catheter procedure to reopen a blocked coronary artery receives an intravenous small-molecule drug that occupies the ligand pocket of platelet fibrinogen-binding integrins. What clinical benefit and primary risk result, and why?
cards.back: Platelets cannot bridge into an artery-blocking clot, and the main risk is bleeding. Occupying the integrin ligand pocket blocks two-ended fibrinogen from cross-linking platelets, pharmacologically mimicking genetic loss of platelet integrins.
cards.why: Eptifibatide and tirofiban act this way on αIIbβ3, predicting the same bleeding risk seen in Glanzmann thrombasthenia.
cards.quote: they keep platelets from bridging. Their main risk is what Glanzmann thrombasthenia predicts: bleeding.
cards.section: How a cell crawls, and what happens when it cannot

cards.front: Why must a circulating leukocyte already keep its integrins in a bent inactive state on the surface rather than synthesising them upon reaching an infection?
cards.back: Arresting on an inflamed vessel wall must occur within about one second, which is far too short to make new protein, so pre-existing surface integrins must switch on rapidly.
cards.quote: A second is too short to make a new protein, so the integrin must already sit on the surface in its bent form
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Trace how a rolling leukocyte converts a local vessel-wall signal into firm integrin arrest within about a second, integrating GPCR, second-messenger, GTPase, and integrin-switching steps.
cards.back: Selectins slow the leukocyte so its GPCR detects wall-bound chemokine and activates PLC, raising Ca2+ and DAG; Ca2+ activates a Rap1 GEF (CalDAG-GEFI in mouse neutrophils), and Rap1-GTP helps bring talin to the β tail so the integrin extends and grips ICAM-1. This rests on fast membrane-localized GPCR signalling driving talin-mediated inside-out activation.
cards.quote: A white-cell G-protein-coupled receptor, a fast architecture whose parts are already at the membrane, detects the chemokine; its G protein activates phospholipase C, raising calcium and diacylglycerol.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A child's white blood cells roll normally on vessel-wall selectins but lack the integrin needed to stop and crawl out into infected tissue (as in LAD-I). What do a blood count and infected tissue sites show, and why?
cards.back: Blood white-cell counts (mostly neutrophils) are very high while infected tissues contain very few neutrophils and form little pus. Leukocytes roll but cannot arrest and exit vessels, trapping them in circulation while depriving wounds of the dead white cells that make pus.
cards.quote: Trapped in circulation, the blood white-cell count (mostly neutrophils) is very high while infected tissue holds very few neutrophils
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In mice, the Ca2+-activated Rap1 GEF CalDAG-GEFI helps bring talin to integrin β tails in both platelets and neutrophils. Predict the combined bleeding and infection phenotype of a mouse lacking CalDAG-GEFI, citing the rules from both blood-cell systems.
cards.back: Impaired platelet clotting (bleeding) and impaired neutrophil arrest on the vessel wall are predicted, because this Rap1 GEF feeds talin activation in both. The lesson notes that other blood cells use other GEFs and details differ, so the prediction holds for cells that depend on it.
cards.why: Without talin-driven switching, platelet αIIbβ3 cannot bridge fibrinogen and leukocyte β2 integrins cannot grip the vessel wall.
cards.quote: Calcium activates a GEF for the Ras-family GTPase Rap1 (CalDAG-GEFI in platelets and mouse neutrophils; other blood cells use other GEFs, and details differ between cell types).
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Humans have 18 integrin α chains and 8 β chains, yet only 24 αβ heterodimers are known, and about one-third of those recognise RGD. How many αβ pairs are theoretically possible, what fraction actually form, and roughly how many human integrins recognise RGD?
cards.back: 18 × 8 = 144 possible αβ pairs; 24 / 144 = 1/6 (about 16.7%) actually form; about 1/3 × 24 = 8 human integrins recognise RGD (leaving roughly 16 non-RGD integrins).
cards.quote: Humans have 18 α chains and 8 β chains, pairing selectively into 24 known integrins (out of 144 possible combinations); about a third recognise RGD.
cards.section: The integrin family in numbers

cards.front: Cells responding to hepatocyte growth factor through c-Met are engineered to lack paxillin, while FAK still recruits Grb2 to activate Ras. What happens to focal-adhesion-localized ERK signalling, and why?
cards.back: Localized ERK activation at the focal adhesion is disrupted. Paxillin acts as the MAP kinase scaffold holding Raf, MEK, and ERK next to FAK so the cascade runs at one address.
cards.quote: paxillin holds Raf, MEK and ERK next to FAK at the focal adhesion, running the familiar cascade at one address.
cards.section: A scaffold for the MAP kinase cascade

cards.front: Purified talin rod bundles unfolded at 29–51 pN in atomic force microscopy and bound up to three vinculin heads at ~12 pN in magnetic tweezers, whereas in living adhesions a vinculin tension sensor reports ~2.5 pN and the weakest talin bundle (R3) opens near 5 pN. What remains unresolved from these measurements?
cards.back: Because lower forces held longer may still unfold bundles, it remains open which talin bundles actually open inside living adhesions, how often they open, and whether stretch-uncovered binding sites are common outside talin.
cards.quote: Which bundles open in living cells, how often, and whether stretch-uncovered sites are common outside talin remain open.
cards.section: Open questions on force inside living adhesions
